tips.tip: Like 'gustar', 'dar cosa' flips the roles: in 'nos da un poco de cosa' the unease is the subject and 'nos' receives it.
'Habría que' – 'hay que' in the conditional: an impersonal we'd-have-to that names no particular doer.
Wanting someone else to act triggers the subjunctive: 'quiere que pongamos', never 'ponemos'.
After conditional 'si' Spanish keeps the present – 'Si funciona' – and saves the future for the result: 'pagaremos'.
'Aunque nos dé' – the subjunctive after 'aunque' treats the extra work as a possibility, not an established fact.
'A Lassie la saca' – when the object opens the sentence, a pronoun must echo it: 'la' doubles Lassie.
'la ruta que hacen' – English can skip that (the route they do), Spanish can't: 'que' always stays in place.
'Subíamos' sets the moving backdrop, 'empezó' fires the event inside it – scene in imperfect, action in preterite.
'no es precisamente relajante' – understatement by 'precisamente': deny the mild word instead of stating the harsh one.
'se dedica a' – 'dedicarse a' is the verb for what someone devotes themselves to, and its 'a' comes built in.
'A Antoine le regalaron' – the receiver is named twice, pronoun and noun: Spanish doubles the indirect object.
'que Beni recoge' – a relative clause can carry its own subject: 'Beni' slots in between 'que' and the verb.
'fue' and 'fuimos' – 'ser' and 'ir' share one preterite table, so only context says which verb you're seeing.
'donde todo era silencio' – after a place, 'donde' does the relative work: no 'en el que' machinery needed.
'no se perdió ni una visita' – 'perderse' means to miss out on something, while plain 'perder' is just to lose.
'Lo que más me gustó' – with 'gustar' the pleaser is the subject, and here it's a whole action: 'ver los ciervos'.
'Hemos viajado' – experience with no date attached: the perfect totals up life so far instead of naming one trip.
'hemos visto de todo' – the perfect keeps a running list open: sightings so far, with more birds free to join.
'venían' – the imperfect for a past routine: they turned up daily, with no start or finish in the frame.
'se quedan un minuto' – 'quedarse' means to stay: without the 'se', 'quedar' covers what remains or where things sit.
'Si dejáramos' pairs with 'tardarían' – imperfect subjunctive for the imagined if, conditional for its result.
'serán herrerillos' – the future used for a guess: probably blue tits, likelihood rather than a forecast.
'son' states what the moles are, 'están dejando' tracks what's currently under way – 'ser' and 'estar' in one line.
'Este año' hasn't finished yet, so the perfect fits: 'han levantado' counts damage inside an open period.
'jura que' – verbs of asserting keep the indicative after 'que': the claim is served up as fact, mood unchanged.
'acababa de alisar' – imperfect 'acabar de' means had just done, and the preterite 'apareció' interrupts it.
'se fueran' – 'si' plus imperfect subjunctive floats the unlikely dream, and 'sería' delivers the would-be result.
'lo confirma' – this 'lo' points at a whole idea, not one noun: Spanish lets a pronoun stand for a clause.
'han pasado de visita' – the perfect flags fresh evidence: the visit is over but its trace is on today's lawn.
'Sin embargo' – the formal however: it sets the whole sentence against the previous one, heavier than 'pero'.
'nos ha puesto' – the perfect because the fallout is still live: 'todavía estamos tratando' ties it to right now.
'Antes' cues the imperfect: 'elegía' and 'tocaba' sketch how things used to run, no end point stated.
'insiste en que' – 'insistir' hangs on to its 'en' even before 'que', and the assertion stays indicative.
'Tres horas dura' – the exclamation fronts the startling bit and lets the verb precede its subject 'la película'.
'Aunque no entendamos' – the subjunctive turns 'aunque' from although into even if: understanding is beside the point.
'dice que encontró' – after 'decir que' the report keeps its indicative, even when the listener has her doubts.
'A Ken le emociona' – 'emocionar' follows the 'gustar' pattern: 'la idea' does the exciting and 'le' marks Ken.
'Si compráramos' – the -ra ending marks the imperfect subjunctive: an unreal purchase, answered by 'meteríamos'.
'querrá' is future in form only – it voices a guess about what Ken currently wants, Spanish's built-in probably.
'lo que se dice convencida' – the set phrase 'lo que se dice' weighs the word it repeats: convinced in the full sense.
'Me pregunto si' frames a wondering, so the future 'hará' reads as speculation about the present, not a prediction.
'quiero que' pushes the verb to 'piense', not 'piensa' – yet the inner belief 'que somos' stays plain indicative.
'que compramos' – that we bought: the relative needs no extra pronoun, the buyer lives in the verb ending.
'esas personas que arreglan' – the relative agrees with 'personas', so plural 'arreglan' even though it's about Ken.
'ha arreglado' – the perfect counts work done up to now, and 'todavía le queda' keeps the job officially open.
'se lo damos a Ken' – 'le' becomes 'se' in front of 'lo': Spanish never lets two l-pronouns sit side by side.
'llamábamos' paints the long-running habit, 'quedó claro' the moment it ended – imperfect versus preterite at work.
'lleva semanas restaurando' – 'llevar' + time + gerund says has-been-doing, all in the present tense, no 'ha' needed.
'se va en la moto' – 'irse' means to head off: the 'se' supplies the leaving, plain 'ir' would want a destination.
'de ahí a' sets up a distance – paired with 'hay un buen trecho', Spanish measures how far one idea is from another.
'habrá ido' – the future perfect guesses about the recent past: where can he have got to, not where he will go.
'A Ken le encanta' – 'encantar' works like 'gustar' but stronger, and what he loves is an infinitive: 'irse por ahí'.
'Ahí va Ken' – the exclamation fronts the place word and the verb lands before its subject: there-goes order.
